items.text: ALKALIS

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 16.5 Ammonia solution is sometimes called ammonium hydroxide. It is an alkali and is used in some cleaning products. Some universal indicator solution has been added to it in the beaker.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ACIDS

items.label: text
items.text: The formulae of some acids are given in Table 16.3.

items.label: text
items.text: All acids contain hydrogen and when acids react the hydrogen shown in red in Table 16.3 is replaced by something else; all acids have replaceable H. For example, when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide we obtain:

items.label: formula
items.text: H C I ( a q ) + N a O H ( a q ) \rightarrow N a C I ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( I )

items.label: text
items.text: The H of the HCl has beenreplaced by an Na.

items.label: text
items.text: Not all of the hydrogens in acids are replaceable, for example in ethanoic acid only the H attached to the O is replaceable, not the ones joined to the C. The reactions of carboxylic acids such as ethanoic acid are discussed further in Chapter 27.

items.label: text
items.text: When acids are in water they dissociate (break apart) to form hydrogen ions (H⁺), for example:

items.label: text
items.text: When we are measuring pH we are actually measuring the concentration of these H+ ions in the solution. This is why the H in pH is written with a capital letter.

items.label: text
items.text: We can define acids as substances that act as a source of hydrogen ions (H⁺) in solution.

items.label: section_header
items.text: BASES

items.label: text
items.text: Bases are substances that neutralise acids by combining with the hydrogen ions in them. When we are referring to a base at this level we usually mean a metal oxide, a metal hydroxide or ammonia (NHg).

items.label: text
items.text: Some bases dissolve in water to form solutions containing hydroxide ions. These are alkalis.

items.label: text
items.text: Alkalis are a source of hydroxide (OH-) ions in solution.

items.label: text
items.text: Examples of alkalis are sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide (all the Group 1 hydroxides). When sodium hydroxide is in water it breaks apart to form sodium and hydroxide ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: N a O H ( a q ) \rightarrow N a ^ { + } ( a q ) + O H ^ { - } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: The other alkali you will meet is a solution of ammonia (NHg). The ammonia reacts with the water to form ammonium ions and hydroxide ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: N H _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \Rightarrow N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } ( a q ) + O H ^ { - } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: These alkalis all have a pH greater than 7.

items.label: section_header
items.text: OTHER ALKALINE SOLUTIONS

items.label: text
items.text: There are some other substances, such as soluble metal carbonates, that react with water to form hydroxide ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: N a _ { 2 } C O _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( I ) \Rightarrow N a O H ( a q ) + N a H C O _ { 3 } ( a q )
